40.0.0.en: 1 Moreover the LORD answered Job, and said, 2 "Shall he that reproveth contend with the Almighty? he that argueth with God, shall he answer him?" 3 Then Job answered the LORD, and said, 4 "Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth. 5 Once have I spoken; but I will not answer: yea, twice; but I will proceed no further."

40.0.1.en: God gave Job the opportunity to answer his questions, but Job could not answer any question. He knew his own weight. For in the days of his greatness and wealth, "the princes refrained talking, and laid their hand on their mouth. The nobles held their peace, and their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth" (Job 29:9-10). Now Job realized the truth about his weight. He said, "Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth" (Job 40:4). The word vile here comes in Hebrew to be translated as trifling or light in weight (without weight, lightweight). What occupied him was not his sins, for he did not say, "I have sinned," but he was like one caught up into the divine mystery, so that he realized the truth about himself before his Creator and the Ruler of his life.

40.0.2.en: Moreover the LORD answered Job, and said, [1]

40.1.0.en: Shall he that reproveth contend with the Almighty? He that argueth with God, shall he answer him? [2]

40.1.1.en: God asks Job: Is it for the creature to dictate his will to his Creator? Or to object to His wisdom and will? It is fitting for a person to answer quickly, rejecting the thought of contending with the Almighty or standing before the wisdom of the Creator.

40.1.2.en: It is as if God were saying to him: Until now you have not grasped My wisdom in My permitting the trial to come upon you. You look at your own loftiness and righteousness, and you have not taken into account My wisdom and My care for you. Did you not learn from the beasts of the wild and the birds of prey to cleave to Me?

40.2.0.en: Then Job answered the LORD, and said, [3]

40.2.1.en: Job was convinced, for his vision of God had passed all bounds, and he now had a worthy appreciation of God's world, with its new horizons, its harmony and its concord.

40.2.2.en: Job now confesses that God can do everything and that His purposes are fulfilled. This melted Job's heart, and he saw himself called to bow beneath the mighty hand of God. Now he submits humbly to the wisdom of God, and by entering into communion with Him he passes into the realm of light and hope. The Lord spoke and His power came, and it brought man's helplessness into true wisdom. When God revealed Himself to Job, He made Job reveal himself. Job gave up his human wisdom, so he left the image of God as a warrior and returned to the image of God as the Friend who came to him in the midst of the tempest. And God became silent again after Job had seen Him.

40.2.3.en: Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee?

40.3.0.en: I will lay mine hand upon my mouth [4].

40.3.1.en: Job surpassed all the people of his time in virtue, and in the dialogue he was able to overcome his friends. But when God spoke with him, he confessed his lowliness and weakness, and was compelled to lay his hand upon his mouth to keep silent in an awesome stillness.

40.3.2.en: Job offers us a lesson in dialogue with God: even if we are righteous in His eyes, we keep silent so that we may not justify ourselves with words, but rather leave our life and practical conduct, by His grace, to speak with Him. Speaking with Him in the language of deeds is better than with the tongue.

40.3.3.en: * The saints have learned to restrain slips of the tongue before the eyes of God, by presenting a good life. They learn to refrain from exaggerated words through the weight of their good works.

40.3.5.en: * Job himself did not keep silent about his sins... Since he is a true worshipper of God, without doubt he made his confession in truth.

40.3.6.en: St. Augustine *Let us consider what man is. The pagans say that he is a rational, mortal animal, capable of reasoning and knowledge. Let us not take our definition of him from them, but from where? From the Holy Scriptures... Hear its words: "That man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil" (Job 1:1). This is truly man! Again another says: "Man is a great thing, and a merciful man is precious" (Prov 20:6) LXX. Those who do not respond to this description will not be able to attain knowledge, and Holy Scripture refuses to recognize them as human beings, but calls them dogs, horses, serpents, foxes and wolves, or any base animal. If this is what man is, then he who lives in pleasures is not a man, for how can he be such who thinks of nothing that befits him? Luxury and dignity cannot be joined together; the one destroys the other. Even the pagans say: {A stuffed belly does not bear a keen mind}.

40.4.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Once have I spoken; but I will not answer: yea, twice; but I will proceed no further [5].

40.4.1.en: In sincere repentance Job says that he spoke once about the trials that had come upon him, without being able to explain the wisdom behind them.

40.4.2.en: I reproached God, and I wanted to enter, as into a trial, and present my case to Him. Perhaps I repeated that, instead of once, twice, but now "I will proceed no further"; I will not repeat what I said before.

40.4.3.en: Job, who had been insisting on a meeting with God in order to dispute with Him, now that he has seen the Lord, falls into an awesome silence.

40.4.4.en: * If we examine the earlier words of the blessed Job, we find that he never uttered anything evil... But when he weighed himself in the perfectly exact balance of God, he confessed that he had sinned in his speech for the second time...

40.4.6.en: * If you confess that you are a sinner, the truth is in you, for the truth itself is light. Your life does not shine with full brightness, because there are sins in you, but when you begin to be enlightened, you come to the confession of sins... First of all, then, confession, and then love. For what is said of love? "Charity shall cover the multitude of sins" (1 Pet 4:8)... Pride quenches love, and humility strengthens it; love extinguishes sins, and humility goes in the company of confession.

40.4.7.en: Tell men who you are, tell God who you are. If you do not tell God who you are, He will judge you for what He finds in you... Do you want Him to forgive you? Know how to say to God: [Hide Thy face from my sins]. Say to Him also the words of the psalmist himself: [I acknowledge my transgression] (Ps 51:3, 9).

40.5.0.en: 6 Then answered the LORD unto Job out of the whirlwind, and said, 7 "Gird up thy loins now like a man: I will demand of thee, and declare thou unto me. 8 Wilt thou also disannul my judgment? wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous? 9 Hast thou an arm like God? or canst thou thunder with a voice like him? 10 Deck thyself now with majesty and excellency; and array thyself with glory and beauty. 11 Cast abroad the rage of thy wrath: and behold every one that is proud, and abase him. 12 Look on every one that is proud, and bring him low; and tread down the wicked in their place. 13 Hide them in the dust together; and bind their faces in secret. 14 Then will I also confess unto thee that thine own right hand can save thee. 15 Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox. 16 Lo now, his strength is in his loins, and his force is in the navel of his belly. 17 He moveth his tail like a cedar: the sinews of his stones are wrapped together. 18 His bones are as strong pieces of brass; his bones are like bars of iron. 19 He is the chief of the ways of God: he that made him can make his sword to approach unto him. 20 Surely the mountains bring him forth food, where all the beasts of the field play. 21 He lieth under the shady trees, in the covert of the reed, and fens. 22 The shady trees cover him with their shadow; the willows of the brook compass him about. 23 Behold, he drinketh up a river, and hasteth not: he trusteth that he can draw up Jordan into his mouth. 24 Can one take him before his eyes? or bore his nose with a snare?"

40.5.1.en: In His second discourse with Job He made clear to him that there is no ground for comparison between the creature and his Creator, and that it is not the creature's right to interrogate his Creator.

40.5.2.en: Then answered the LORD unto Job out of the whirlwind, and said, [6]

40.5.3.en: Gird up thy loins now like a man.

40.6.0.en: I will demand of thee, and declare thou unto me [7].

40.7.0.en: The Septuagint rendering of verse [8] is: "Dost thou think that I have dealt with thee for any other purpose than that thou mightest appear righteous?" It is as if God were revealing to Job, with all power, His transcendent care and His love for him: if He permitted him trials of such magnitude, their aim was only that Job might be justified and enjoy victory over the devil.

40.7.1.en: When Job defends himself against the blows that God permitted to come upon him, he accuses divine justice; but if he accepts the trial with thanksgiving, God justifies him and glorifies him, and it is reckoned not as his chastisement but as his approval.

40.7.2.en: * He who struggles in defending himself against the blows of God seeks to ignore the judgments of God who inflicted the blows. And when he says that he was not struck on account of his faults, what does he do but accuse the One who strikes? The blows from heaven did not fall upon the blessed Job to remove his faults, but rather to add to his merits, so that he who in time of calm shone with such great holiness might thus declare the virtue of patience hidden within him... But he thought that he had been struck unjustly when he found nothing in himself that required correction. So that he might not be puffed up with pride in his innocence, the divine voice rebuked him, while his mind was free from evil but he was weighed down with blows, and he was called to the mysteries of the divine judgments... So the saint was not at variance with God in any sin, but was in agreement with Him, though with some difficulty because of the blows.

40.7.4.en: Wilt thou also disannul my judgment?

40.7.5.en: Wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous? [8]

40.7.6.en: * At the end of the struggles He (God) proclaimed the victory of the wrestler in a sublime declaration, and revealed the mystery of his sorrows, saying: ["Dost thou think that I have dealt with thee for any other purpose than that thou mightest appear righteous?"] This is the balm of his wounds, this is the crown of the struggle, this is the reward of his patience.

40.7.7.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus *The righteous endure trial here, because they are sojourners and strangers, and in a foreign city. The righteous endure those things for the sake of testing. What did God say to Job? [Do you not suppose that I warn you for any other purpose than that you may appear righteous?] (Job 40:8) LXX. But sinners, when they suffer any affliction, suffer only the punishment for their sins. Therefore in all circumstances, whether bitter or not, let us give thanks to God. For both conditions are profitable. For God does nothing out of hatred or enmity toward us, but what He does is out of His care and concern for us.

40.7.8.en: St. John Chrysostom *Had Job not fought in the battle and gained the victory, he would not have received the crown of righteousness, and would not have heard the Lord say: Do you not think that I speak with you for any purpose other than that you may appear righteous? (Job 40:8 LXX).

40.7.9.en: St. Jerome *I think that the wind means trials. For trials show that in the heap of believers some are like chaff and others like wheat. When your soul is overcome by some trial, the trial does not turn you into chaff. Rather, because you are chaff, light in weight and unbelieving, the trial reveals what you are and what you had hidden. On the contrary, when you bear trials courageously, the trials do not make you a believer and a patient man, but rather reveal the virtues of patience and courage which were hidden in you. The Lord says: "Dost thou think that I warn thee for any other reason than that thou mayest appear righteous" (Job 40:8 LXX).

40.8.0.en: Origen Hast thou an arm like God? or canst thou thunder with a voice like him? [9]

40.8.1.en: God reproaches Job, saying that there is no ground for comparison between the arm of the Lord and His voice, and the arm of Job and his voice. For God is mighty in His work and mighty in His words.

40.8.2.en: * When speaking of the voice of God and His arm, let us take great care lest our mind imagine something material in Him. For he who confines within the frame of a body Him who is immaterial, who fills all and embraces all, falls into the heresy of the Anthropomorphites (likening the Godhead to man). But Almighty God, in drawing us near to Himself, humbles Himself to teach us the high things and condescends to the lowly things... Therefore in His Holy Scripture He sometimes uses likenesses taken now from human bodies, now from our minds, and sometimes even from birds...

40.9.0.en: Deck thyself now with majesty and excellency; and array thyself with glory and beauty [10].

40.9.1.en: A man may adorn himself with a garment of glory and splendor, so that he awes other men and draws the great to himself as friends, but this is worth nothing before the glory and majesty of God.

40.9.2.en: * God surrounds Himself with beauty, of which it is written: "The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty" (Ps 93:1). He is exalted on high in us when we are sure that His nature cannot be searched out by our minds. He is glorious, He who contains joy and has no need of praise. He is wrapped in beautiful garments, for He appoints the orders of the holy angels to the service of His beauty. He created them and established His Church as a glorious garment, without spot or wrinkle. Therefore it was said to Him by the prophet: "Thou art clothed with honour and majesty: who coverest thyself with light as with a garment" (Ps 104:1-2).

40.10.0.en: Cast abroad the rage of thy wrath: and behold every one that is proud, and abase him [11].

40.10.1.en: It is as though He were saying to him: "There is no ground for comparison between Me and you; if you were in a state of anger and wrath, could you, with a look from you, shatter your arrogant opponents?" For it is said: "For the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up; and he shall be brought low" (Isa 2:12). No proud man can stand before His gaze.

40.10.2.en: If Job silenced his friends to some extent in the long dialogue and for a long time, then a single look from God shakes the whole being of the proud who exalt themselves against Him.

40.11.0.en: Look on every one that is proud, and bring him low; and tread down the wicked in their place [12].

40.11.1.en: It is as though God were saying to Job: "I know that your request was not out of arrogance and pride. I know your humble heart, even if you reproached Me in your distress and asked for an explanation of what had befallen you. If you were distressed because of your friends' arrogance toward you and their unjust accusation of you, do not fear. If you wish, I have permitted you to look at them with the eye of faith, and you will overcome them. You can overcome the wicked and proud in their places before they move to face your gaze.

40.11.2.en: If they think that they are more honorable or richer or happier than you, because what befell you did not befall them, they will be crushed, and their temporal glories, their material resources and their offspring will not profit them.

40.11.3.en: * The proud are confounded at the look of the Lord, whether here, where in His mercy He reveals their faults and condemns them, or there, where He punishes them by His justice. But pride itself is the place of the wicked. It is written: [Pride is the beginning of all sin] (Sir 10:15), for it dwells in the place where evil dwells, though it is very hard to distinguish between evil and pride. He who is very proud thinks evil of our Creator. The wicked man, then, is trodden down in his place, for he is shattered by the very pride that lifted him up... Often, while the proud man advances in his vain glory against God, he sinks inwardly into real misery.

40.11.5.en: * I do not want you to be proud on account of anything, but rather to be fearful. You travel like a young girl with gold. Let her fear the thief. This temporal life is a race. Here we compete so that we may be crowned afterward. No one enters among serpents and scorpions while sure that he will be safe.

40.11.6.en: * Not only fornication and prostitution defile those who practice them, but pride also defiles a man more than they do.

40.11.7.en: * Humility is given to each person according to the measure of his greatness. Pride is harmful to everyone. It seeks to corrupt, above all, those who are great!

40.11.8.en: St. Jerome * It is clear that excessive boasting was one of the marks of the false apostles.

40.11.9.en: * Arrogance together with sin is a great calamity... If he who does good loses his labor if he becomes puffed up, how great is the iniquity of him who adds to his sins the sin of arrogance? For such a one cannot practice repentance.

40.12.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Hide them in the dust together; and bind their faces in secret [13].

40.12.1.en: While the proud think that they have overcome and triumphed, God asks Job not to fear them, but to hide them in the dust, to bury them as in a dark tomb, so that their names are no longer remembered. It is like Moses the prophet, who hid the proud Egyptian in the sand (Ex 2:12).

40.12.2.en: Their faces are bound in the darkness, where they cannot stand before God, the true Light, but go down into the outer darkness, the darkness of Hades.

40.12.3.en: * God, by His just judgment, hides the proud and the wicked in the dust, by permitting their hearts to be swallowed up by earthly things according to their own choice, as they despise the love of their Creator.

40.12.4.en: Fittingly He adds: [and at the same time I bind their faces in the pit]... since He brings down the intention of their hearts when it wants to exalt itself over men. For he whose face is turned down toward Hades looks upon the lowly things.

40.12.6.en: * What madness! Does this proud man not know that his glory passes away and evaporates like a dream, and that greatness and authority are nothing but a deceptive mirage?

40.13.0.en: St. Basil the Great Then will I also confess unto thee that thine own right hand can save thee [14].

40.13.1.en: God wants to praise His creature; He treasures him and seeks his honor. But can Job, despite God's testimony to his uprightness, save himself by his arm or by his right hand, that is, by his own strength? He who makes light of God's support of him relies on his own strength, and so does not receive praise from God.

40.13.2.en: It is fitting for the believer to sing: "For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance, because thou hadst a favour unto them" (Ps 44:3).

40.13.3.en: * At the moment when we are still in the midst of the battle, fighting and being wounded, we ask ourselves: Who is the victor?

40.13.4.en: The victor, brethren, is the one who relies on God, who supports him as he fights, and does not rely on his own strength. Satan has his experience in war, but if God is with us we shall overcome him. Satan fights by himself, and if we try to do the same, he will overcome us. He is an experienced fighter, and so it is fitting for us to call upon the Almighty to stand against him.

40.13.5.en: Let Him who is never overcome dwell in you, and you will overcome him who is accustomed to conquer. Whom does he overcome? Those whose hearts are empty of God.

40.13.6.en: * God knows your striving and your good will, and awaits your struggle, and supports your weakness, and crowns your victory.

40.13.7.en: St. Augustine Behold now the sea horse (behemoth), which I made with thee.

40.14.0.en: He eateth grass as an ox [15].

40.14.1.en: Behemoth comes in the plural form of "behemah," that is, an animal. It is still used in Egypt to mean a tame animal such as sheep, donkeys, horses and so on, and it differs from the Hebrew word chaytow, which is for the wild beasts of the field.

40.14.2.en: Some see that it refers here to the sea horse, the barniq, or the sea buffalo, the hippopotamus.

40.14.3.en: Adam Clarke considers this animal to be one of the extinct animals, called the mammoth.

40.14.4.en: This animal is distinguished by the hugeness of its body together with its strength, so that no man can enter into a wrestling match with it; how then does he wish to resist his Creator?

40.14.5.en: Some thought that it refers here to the elephant because of the hugeness of its body and its strength, but many scholars have rejected that.

40.14.6.en: St. John Chrysostom says that some interpreters interpreted this passage in a spiritual sense, and that this animal refers to Satan.

40.14.7.en: If it refers to Satan, then he eats grass like the ox, meaning that when the body dominates the human soul, man becomes like the grass of the field, food for Satan!

40.14.8.en: God dwelt at length in His discourse with Job on behemoth, a symbol of the enemy of good, the devil. Perhaps He wanted to direct Job's gaze to this enemy. Instead of murmuring against the judgments of God, it is fitting for Job to realize that there is a dangerous enemy who wants to devour all mankind, and that it was he who asked permission to tempt him; but these trials turn the devil into a plaything that even little children mock.

40.14.9.en: * The demon of fornication stirs up bodily lust, and launches his attack upon the ascetics, and strives to make them abandon their asceticism, sowing in their souls the thought that this asceticism of theirs is of no use.

40.14.10.en: And if he is able to defile the soul, he begins to prepare it to speak and to hear certain (evil) conversations, so that it seems as though the (evil) act itself were present before their eyes.

40.15.0.en: St. Mar Evagrius of Pontus Lo now, his strength is in his loins, and his force is in the navel of his belly [16].

40.15.1.en: He refers here to its surpassing power despite the hugeness of its body: its strength is in its loins (the hips), and its force in the navel of its belly.

40.15.2.en: The strength of the elephant is in its neck, of the lion in its claws, of the horse and the ox in their chests, but the main strength of this animal is in its loins. It was said in Nahum: "Make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily" (Nah 2:1).

40.15.3.en: It is fitting for the believer to mortify his loins, and not allow the flesh to lust against the Spirit (Gal 5:17).

40.15.4.en: * If we want to eat the flesh of the Lamb, we must mortify our loins, that is, the works of the flesh, and destroy in ourselves what Job said of Satan: "Lo now, his strength is in his loins, and his force is in the navel of his belly" (Job 40:16). It is fitting that we not allow the flesh to lust against the Spirit (Gal 5:17), but through the Spirit mortify the deeds of the flesh, and by this purification enjoy the body of the Lamb.

40.15.5.en: St. Jerome In a letter to Eustochium, St. Jerome wrote, explaining that asceticism is not of value in itself, but is an important means for self-control and chastity.

40.15.6.en: * The Creator, the Lord of all, takes no pleasure in rumbling and an empty stomach..... but these are necessary as a means of preserving chastity. Job was dear to God, perfect and upright before Him (Job 2:3), and yet hear what he says about Satan: [His strength is in his loins (his sexual organs), and his force is in the navel] (Job 40:16). I chose these expressions for the sake of delicacy of speech, but what is meant by them is the reproductive sexual organs of both sexes. The descendant of David, who sits on his throne according to the promise, is said to be of the fruit of his belly (his loins) (Ps 132:11). And the seventy-five souls of the family of Jacob who came into Egypt are said to have come out of his loins (Gen 46:26). So when the hollow of Jacob's thigh was put out of joint as he wrestled with the Lord, he ceased to beget children. Again the Israelites were commanded to celebrate the Passover with loins girded and mortified (Ex 12:11). God said to Job: "Gird up now thy loins like a man" (Job 38:3). John wore a girdle of a skin (Mt 3:4). And the Apostles were bound to gird their loins in order to carry the lamp of the Gospel (Lk 12:35). When Ezekiel told us of Jerusalem that she was found in the open field, covered with blood, he used the words: [thy navel was not cut] (Ezek 16:4-6). Therefore Satan, in his attack on men, has his strength in his loins, and in his attack on women his force is in the navel. Do you want proof of these assertions of mine? Take examples of it. Samson was more courageous than a lion and steadier than a rock..... but in the presence of his guide his resistance vanished and was blotted out. David was a man whose heart was after the likeness of God's heart, whose lips were always praising the Holy One, the Christ who was to come, and yet, as he walked on the roof of his house, the temptation of Bathsheba's nakedness caught him, and he added murder to the crime of adultery. Observe how a man, even in his own house, cannot use his eyes without danger staring him in the face.

40.15.7.en: St. Jerome * And it is also clear to all that adultery is committed only by a bodily act, for God says of this blessed husband Job: "Lo now, his strength is in his loins, and his force is in the navel of his belly" (Job 40:16).

40.15.8.en: Abba Serapion He moveth his tail like a cedar.

40.16.0.en: The sinews of his stones are wrapped together [17].

40.16.1.en: He moves his tail like a strong cedar tree, and it was said of the dragon: "His tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven, and did cast them to the earth" (Rev 12:4).

40.16.2.en: He is strong; when he treads upon a man with his feet he crushes him, for "the sinews of his stones are wrapped together."

40.16.3.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh portrays for us how the devil cannot bear the salvation of man. When he sees a sinner walking the path of repentance, he asks his soldiers to intensify their efforts to shatter him by evil thoughts and vain glory and by every possible means. The saint wrote to two harlots named Lantia and Maria, who had repented and become recluses, warning them of the devil's wars and his resistance to them with all violence.

40.16.4.en: * Now the commander of the harmful forces of the left (the devil commands his soldiers) orders because of his enmity toward you both:

40.16.5.en: Do not fight the pure, nor the perfect, nor any of my strong enemies, but these two who were my own, and despised me and mocked me. And they stand in the rank of the saints.

40.16.6.en: Bring upon them pieces of despair, fill them with sloth.

40.16.7.en: Sow envy in them toward one another, that they may submit to weakness and burn with the desire for food.

40.16.8.en: Awaken their thoughts to love their former deeds. Trouble them with thoughts of fornication.

40.16.9.en: Hinder their prayers, lest they be strong enough to fulfill their vows...

40.16.10.en: Set them on the edge of the precipice of greatness, and bind them with love of glory...

40.16.11.en: Lead them to think that they have become good.

40.16.12.en: Send the sick to them that they may pray for them, and urge others to say: We were healed by your prayers; deceive them into thinking that they are not penitents but virtuous women.

40.17.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh His bones are as strong pieces of brass; his bones are like bars of iron (and his ribs are like beaten iron) [18].

40.17.1.en: No one can break his bones, nor tear his ribs apart; his bones are like pipes of brass, and his ribs like beaten iron.

40.17.2.en: * What does the Book of Job say about him? He is fearful and terrifying (Job 40:18; 41:7). His sides are brass, and his back is cast iron, his bowels are of sharp stones. This and more the Holy Scripture says about him. This is the great and mighty leader of the satanic hosts. But what does the One who has the true and unique power call him? He is a "little fox!" (Song 2:15). All who are with Satan, his whole force, are an object of mockery. God calls them by the same name, "the little foxes," and urges the hunters against them.

40.17.3.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa He is the chief of the ways of God.

40.18.0.en: He that made him can make his sword to approach unto him [19].

40.18.1.en: The text in the Septuagint reads: [This is the first of the works of the Lord, made to be mocked by His angels]. Some have relied on this passage in claiming that Satan was created evil and did not fall by his own will. St. Augustine refuted this view in his book "The Literal Meaning of Genesis."

40.18.2.en: Who denies that God created the devil from among the greatest of the heavenly orders, but by his own will he became a laughingstock and an object of mockery to the angels?

40.18.3.en: * It is said of Satan [the beginning of the works of the Lord, made to be mocked by His angels], not because he is the first creature that God brought into being, nor because he was an evil creature from the beginning. But God, knowing that he would come to have an evil will inclined to harm the good, created him to be of use to the good. This is the meaning of the words [His angels mock him], for Satan is mocked when he tries to destroy the one whom he chose by his own will, who proves useful to the servants of God despite his evil intent. Truly God saw that when He created him.

40.18.4.en: St. Augustine The devil was a great and distinguished star among the heavenly beings, "Lucifer, son of the morning" (Isa 14:12). He not only enjoyed light but shone with his light on others as a bright light in the morning, as a divine gift. But he exalted himself against God, his Creator and the Giver of light, and thought that he could rise to the level of God Himself, even to become greater than He, so he fell and became darkness instead of light, having separated himself by himself from God, the source of light. He wanted to sit upon the mount of Zion (Ps 48:2), the holy mountain of God, reckoning himself as God in greatness, and so he exalted himself above the clouds!

40.18.5.en: * Those who say that Satan is not God's creature are mistaken. Insofar as he is Satan he is not God's creature, but the being himself (as a creature) is God's creature. It is like saying that a murderer is not God's creature, but as a man he is God's creature.

40.18.6.en: *It is perfectly clear from these words (Isa 14:12) that he who was formerly Lucifer, who appeared in the morning, fell from heaven. For if he were - as some claim - a being of darkness, why was it said of him that he was like Lucifer, or the light-bearer? Or how does he who has no light at all rise in the morning?

40.18.7.en: Origen * The saying of the Lord Christ: "The prince of this world," means by it the devil, and wicked men have called him by this name, not because he rules heaven and earth, for otherwise he would overturn and reverse creation, but because he rules those who have surrendered themselves to him.

40.18.8.en: St. John Chrysostom * We understand from these words that there is one King, who is the Creator of the whole universe. On the other side there is the prince of this world, who calls himself the king of darkness. Myriads of angels serve the true King, while myriads of demons surround the prince of the powers of darkness (Col 1:13). The principalities and powers and virtue follow the King of kings and Lord of lords. And in the end, when Christ delivers up the kingdom to God the Father, after He has put down all rule and all authority and power of the enemy, it is necessary that He reign till He has put all enemies under His feet (1 Cor 15:24-25).

40.19.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa Surely the mountains bring him forth food, where all the beasts of the field play [20].

40.19.1.en: Some see here the marvelous goodness of God: for despite the hugeness of this animal's body and its power, it is not a predator like the lion or the leopard. Were it a predator living on the flesh of animals, then with the hugeness of its body it would need to devour many animals, because it needs an enormous quantity of food. But its food is the grass which is found in abundance on the mountains. And since it lives on vegetation, the beasts of the field, which are weaker than it in body, do not fear it, but play with it.

40.20.0.en: He lieth under the shady trees, in the covert of the reed, and fens [21].

40.20.1.en: * The great trees shade him (Satan), and he sleeps beside the reeds and the rushes and the papyrus (Job 40:21). He is king over all the things that are in the waters, that is, over the throne of pleasure and luxury.

40.20.2.en: St. Jerome The shady trees cover him with their shadow.

40.21.0.en: The willows of the brook compass him about [22].

40.21.1.en: Since the beasts of the field play with him, he has no need to lurk in dark places or hide in caves in order to pounce suddenly upon his prey. Rather he lies down in safety under the shady trees. He sleeps in peace, and the animals gather around him rejoicing, playing with him.

40.21.2.en: Since he harms no one, he has no need of caves to protect him, but is covered by the reeds and other plants that grow beside the waters.

40.21.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us a symbolic interpretation of this passage, saying: [Behemoth finds a kind of rest in those who become cold by withdrawing from the light of the true Sun, and so it is said of him, "he sleeps under the shade"... The moist places (the willows of the brook) are the minds of earthly men, where there is the moisture of fleshly lusts. In these minds he plants the footprints of his wickedness, and he sinks into their minds as into moist ground. The moist places are the works of lust. For the foot does not slip on dry ground, but only when it walks on slippery ground, where it is hard to be supported. Those who cannot stand upright pass through this life in moist places].

40.21.4.en: Behold, he drinketh up a river, and hasteth not.

40.22.0.en: He trusteth that he can draw up Jordan into his mouth [23].

40.22.1.en: Since this huge animal needs an enormous quantity of water, one imagines that it is able to drink a whole river. If the river overflows, it does not flee, but deliberately drinks from it without fear or alarm.

40.22.2.en: Behemoth thinks that he is able to drink up the whole river Jordan if it were poured into his mouth.

40.22.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the waters refer to the peoples. The devil opened his mouth to drink the whole river, that is, the whole human race, as his drink, and it is his right to swallow them up. And when the Lord Christ came to the river Jordan, the enemy opened his mouth to drink up the Jordan with the Lord descending into it. In vain the enemy tried to catch the Lord Christ; rather the Lord Christ crushed the head of the dragon in the waters of the Jordan.

40.22.4.en: The enemy still opens his mouth to swallow the whole river Jordan, that is, to catch those who have received the sacrament of Baptism and become children of God, but in their negligence he deceives them into returning to sonship to the devil.

40.22.5.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem spoke of the gift of Baptism as liberation from the authority of the devil, the beast who dwells in the depths of the waters, saying: [It is written in Job that there was in the waters the beast who "trusteth that he can draw up Jordan into his mouth" (Job 40:23), and his heads had to be broken (Ps 74:14). Therefore the Lord went down and bound the strong one in the waters, that we may receive strength in them, since we have authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions (Lk 10:19). The beast was great and terrifying, "a thick vessel could not bear one scale of his tail" (Job 41:7) LXX, raging against everyone who met him. "Life" went down to him to meet him, and there shut the mouth of death, and then we are saved, saying: O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? (1 Cor 15:55). The sting of death has been removed by Baptism! Here you are entering the waters carrying your sins, and by the invocation of grace, as we seal your souls, the terrifying beast will no longer swallow you.]

40.22.6.en: Can one take him before his eyes?

40.23.0.en: Or bore his nose with a snare? [24]

40.23.1.en: What is the snare that pierces the nose of the enemy of good? Pope Gregory (the Great) says: [What are they but the earnest counsels of the saints? They pierce the nostrils of this behemoth... The Lord pierces his nostrils with snares, when He takes away his strength, breaking the cunning of deception by the firm understandings of the saints].

40.23.2.en: How marvelous! God permits the existence of the devil, and does not take me from before him. For He knows that through Him I overcome him. I strike his arrogant nose with the spear of the Cross and I shatter it. By the Spirit of the Lord I live victorious and triumphant. I sing in the spirit of victory over Satan who fell from heaven like lightning!

40.23.3.en: * Satan aims arrows against me, but I have a sword with me.

40.23.4.en: He has a bow with him, but I am a soldier bearing heavy arms...

40.23.5.en: He is a bearer of the bow, but he does not dare to come near me, for he casts his arrows from afar.

40.23.6.en: *You lost Paradise, but God gave you heaven, so that He might confirm His tenderness, and that He defeats the devil, showing that even if he perfects tens of thousands of plots against the human race, they will not profit him, for God always leads us to a greater honor.

40.23.7.en: You lost Paradise (the garden of Eden), and God opened heaven to you.

40.23.8.en: You fell under the sentence of toil for a time, and you have been honored with life eternally.

40.23.9.en: God commands the earth to bring forth thorns and thistles, but the soil of the Spirit brings forth fruit for you. Do you not see that the gain is greater than the loss?

40.23.10.en: St. John Chrysostom * Paul tells them to be brave and strong like the wrestler and the soldier of Christ, doing everything with love for God and for one another.

40.23.11.en: St. Didymus the Blind * Let us put on our heads the helmet of salvation, so that we may not be wounded and die in the battle.

40.23.12.en: Let us gird our loins with truth, that we may not be found weak in the fight.

40.23.13.en: Let us arise and awaken Christ, and He will calm the waves for us.

40.23.14.en: Let us take the shield against the Evil One, as a preparation for the Gospel of our Savior (Eph 6:15-16).

40.23.15.en: Let us receive from our Lord the authority to reign over serpents and scorpions (Lk 10:19)...

40.23.16.en: Let us rejoice in our hope at all times (Rom 12:12), that He who is our hope and our Savior may rejoice in us...

40.23.17.en: Let us take for ourselves a weapon for the battle (Eph 6:16), which is the preparation of the Gospel.

40.23.18.en: Let us knock at the door of heaven (Mt 7:7), and it will be opened to us and we shall enter in.

40.23.19.en: Let us ask for mercy diligently, and we shall receive what is necessary for us.

40.23.20.en: Let us seek His kingdom and His righteousness (Mt 6:33).

40.23.21.en: Let us meditate on what is above, on the heavenly things, where Christ ascended and is glorified.

40.23.22.en: But let us forget the world which is not ours, until we reach the place to which we are called.

40.23.23.en: Let us lift up our eyes on high, to see the transfigured radiance.

40.23.24.en: Let us lift up our wings like eagles, to see where the carcase is (Mt 24:28)...

40.23.25.en: Our enemy is skillful, my dear, and the one who fights us is crafty. He prepares himself to attack the brave and victorious, to make them weak. But his own feeble ones he does not fight, for they are captives delivered up to him.

40.23.26.en: He who has two wings flies away from him with them, so that the arrows he hurls toward him do not reach him.

40.23.27.en: The spiritual see him fighting, and his weapon has no power over their bodies.

40.23.28.en: All the children of light do not fear him, for darkness flees from before the light. The children of the Good One do not fear the evil one, for He has given them to tread upon him with their feet (Gen 3:15).

40.23.29.en: St. Aphrahat * No sin arising from satanic affliction was able to approach the body of the Lord. The Lord stood firm against the enemy's temptations, in order to restore victory to mankind. He made Satan a plaything, as David proclaimed: "There is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein" (Ps 104:26), and also: [He shall break in pieces the false accuser] (Ps 72:4). And also [Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in the waters] (Ps 74:13-14). And in the Book of Job the Lord declared that this leviathan would become a plaything and be caught in this trial, saying: "Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook?" (Job 41:1).

40.23.31.en: Who will rescue me from the devil but You?

40.23.32.en: * In the midst of my afflictions my soul is embittered.

40.23.33.en: I enter with You into bitter reproach.

40.23.34.en: I forget the truth about myself, that I am lowly dust before a great Creator.

40.23.35.en: * I have sinned in my thinking as in my words.

40.23.36.en: I spoke once and twice, I asked: Why do You prosper the way of the wicked?

40.23.37.en: Why do You permit afflictions to come upon me?

40.23.38.en: But I will proceed no further with words.

40.23.39.en: I am silent before You; Your arm is strong and Your voice thunders.

40.23.40.en: Your majesty and splendor, who can describe them? * I have discovered the truth of my weak self, and I have come to know the violence of the devil, my enemy.

40.23.41.en: Who will raise me up but You?

40.23.42.en: Who will deliver me from this enemy but You, O Lover of mankind?

40.23.43.en: * Strengthen me, that I may mortify my loins, and not allow the lusts of the flesh to destroy the desires of the Spirit.

40.23.44.en: The strength of the enemy is in his loins and the navel of his belly!

40.23.45.en: Keep me from him, and sanctify my loins and my belly.

40.23.46.en: * You created him a shining star, and in his wickedness he descended to Hades.

40.23.47.en: He wants to draw me down with him.

40.23.48.en: Who will deliver me from him but You?

40.23.49.en: He opens his mouth to swallow all the children of men.

40.23.50.en: Would that I might hide in You, so that he does not come near me.

40.23.51.en: May I enjoy Your Cross, and so pierce his nose.

40.23.52.en: May I live by Your Holy Spirit, and break his arrogant nose!
